Living curves

In the first sketches, two strokes, clay and sage, rise from one base to one tip and cross on the way. Here we take that mark and try to make it look more like a plant: thicker where it starts, finer where it ends, less even, with tips that curl or open into a leaf.

As before, every tile shows the mark at logo size, then at 32 and 16 pixels. The marks below come from notknowing-garden.living/stems, which draws each stem as a filled band around a centre line, rather than as a line of one width.

The logo

The one we chose: the tapered pair from section B, tips apart, with the clay stem reaching higher and the sage stem stopping lower. It is notknowing-garden.living/logo, and clojure -M:build writes it to svg/logo.svg, svg/logo-ink.svg and two wordmarks.

logo
logo, ink
logo, horizontal

The rest of this notebook is how we got there.

Where we start

two-curves, twist 0.85, weight 8

A. From lines to ribbons

First we redraw the same two curves as filled bands. At one width the band matches the line. Then we let the width fall from the base to the tip: w is the width at the base, tip-w at the tip, and a larger taper keeps the stem full for longer before it thins.

one width, 8
12 to 1.2
13 to 1, taper 2
12 to 1, taper 1.6

Where the two stems leave the base, their full widths overlap in a lump. foot narrows the very bottom, so each stem swells up out of a fine point, the way a brush stroke does when it first touches the paper.

foot 1
foot 0.7
foot 0.45
foot 0.2

A tapered stroke already looks less like a diagram and more like a stem. With both tips meeting at one point, though, it still closes like a flame or a bulb.

B. Tips apart, and a lean

Plants are rarely mirror images. Here each stem gets its own tip, so one stops lower and the other reaches higher and further out.

tips [[50 10] [50 10]]
tips [[56 8] [44 14]]
tips [[60 6] [38 20]]
tips [[64 4] [34 26]]

The tips apart make the mark open at the top. At the widest setting the two stems look like a pair of horns, so we stay near the third.

Two ways to lean. lean turns the whole drawing about its base; bow bends it, a little low down and more toward the top. The turned versions look tilted, like a sign hung crooked; the bowed ones look more like a stem that grew toward one side.

lean -8°
lean 8°
bow -10
bow 10

C. Tendrils

curl carries a stem on past its tip, turning more and more tightly, as a pea tendril winds. turn is the total turn in degrees; its sign sets the direction.

sage, -300°
sage, +300°
clay, +360°
clay, -360°

Both stems curling. Curls of different sizes look more like growth than a matched pair; when both turn inward the clay one becomes a hook, close to a question mark.

both, matched
both, different
both inward
longer, tighter

At 16 pixels the curls are gone: they are finer than a pixel. We come back to small sizes in section H.

D. Leaves and buds

A leaf can grow out of the side of a stem (at is how far along), or the stem can open into a leaf at its end.

leaf at the sage tip
pale sage leaf
side leaf, sage
two side leaves

The leaf at the end of the sage stem reads at once as a seedling. The pale leaf separates from its stem and looks laid on top. Small side leaves look like thorns or fins at this scale, so we drop them.

We also tried a bud: the stem swells again near its end. It came out looking like a spoon.

bud on the clay stem

E. Over and under

Where the stems cross, the one on top can cut a thin gap in the one behind, as in a woven or plaited drawing. over picks which stem is on top and gap sets the width of the cut. The gap is a mask, so the ground shows through it, whatever the ground is.

no weave
clay over, gap 1.4
sage over, gap 1.1
sage over, gap 2.2

In two colours the weave adds a fine paper line; without it the colours alone tell the stems apart. In one colour the weave is what tells them apart, which matters for a logo that has to print in one ink.

ink, no weave
ink, weave
sage, no weave
sage, weave

With one crossing, whichever stem passes behind looks cut in two. Sage over clay keeps the lower sage lobe whole, which balances the longer clay stem, so we keep that.

F. Irregularity

wobble moves the centre line sideways by a few units, smoothly and not at the ends; grain varies the width by a few percent. Both come from slow sine waves with phases drawn from a seed, so the same seed always gives the same drawing. spread lets one lower lobe be wider than the other.

spread [1 1], wobble 0, seed 7
spread [1.1 0.9], wobble 1.5, seed 3
spread [1.1 0.9], wobble 1.5, seed 9
spread [1.1 0.9], wobble 1.5, seed 21
grain 0
grain 0.08
grain 0.15
grain 0.3

At 0.3 the grain turns lumpy. Around 0.1 the edges get a slight unevenness, like a brush stroke, without drawing the eye.

G. Tried and set aside

Roots: each stem carries on a little below the base, so the two cross there too. Ground: a short tapered line under the base. Twining: the two stems wind around each other several times. A multiply blend, so the overlap darkens.

roots
ground
twining, 3 half-turns
multiply blend

The roots look like legs or tentacles, and the ground makes a small mound that reads as an illustration rather than a sign. Twining looks like rope or a chain, and its many cuts turn to noise when small. Clay multiplied by sage is nearly black, so the overlap becomes a dark spot.

H. Small sizes

The tall mark is less than half as wide as it is high, so at 16 pixels it is about seven pixels wide, and its thin tips vanish. For small sizes we draw a shorter, wider and heavier version.

Heavy bands bring a problem: where a stem bends more tightly than half its width, the inner edge of the band folds back over itself. We cover the holes this leaves with discs, but the outline still grows ears at the tips and base. Drawing each stem as thirty short stroked runs, each at its own width with round ends, avoids the folding, at the cost of slightly scalloped edges, which do not show at 32 pixels.

heavy, as an outline
heavy, as stroked runs
runs, no curls
runs, weight 22
reference, weight 12
small, woven
small, ink, woven
small, clay, woven

I. Colour

The tendril pair and the leaf pair in four pairings of the site's colours. (The one-colour versions are in section E.)

clay + sage
two sages
clay + pale sage
ink + clay
clay + sage
two sages
clay + pale sage

Two sages are the calmest; clay and sage keep the two people distinct. Ink and clay look heavier and more formal.

paper
clay + pale sage
paper, leaf
clay + pale sage, leaf

On the dark ground the woven gap shows the dark through it, since it is a mask rather than a paper-coloured line.

J. Candidates

Our strongest few. The first three are for logo sizes, the first two in clay and sage and the third in two sages. The fourth and fifth are small-size versions, in colour and in one ink. The last is the tendril pair in one ink.

2. leaf and tendril, clay + sage
3. tendrils, two sages
4. small, clay + sage
5. small, ink, woven
